teaser: Three bodies, one block of marble, and not a single side you could call the front.
review_notes:
The photo is taken from below and shows the upper two thirds of the group from one side; the young man's head is hidden and the base is out of frame. Only what this view shows is pointed at.
Height about 4.1 m, single block of marble; set up in the Loggia dei Lanzi in January 1583 (finished 1582).
Giambologna born Jean de Boulogne in Douai, Flanders, 1529; in Italy from about 1550.
Carved without a fixed subject; the title is credited to the writer Raffaello Borghini; a bronze relief of the Sabine story was added to the base.
Full-size plaster model kept at the Galleria dell'Accademia, Florence.
Often described as the first large sculpture group designed with no principal viewpoint.
Bernini's Rape of Proserpina dated 1621 to 1622.
A dangling foot visible at left center of the photo was left out because it is unclear whose it is from this angle.

lesson.text: One. That is the number of blocks of marble in this sculpture. Three intertwined bodies, stacked more than 4 meters high (about 13.5 feet), with arms flung into empty air, and no joins anywhere. If the chisel had slipped once near the top, there was no gluing it back.

You are seeing it the way a passerby does in Florence: from the pavement of the main square, head tipped back, with a palace behind. From here the young man who does the lifting is mostly a back. That is fine. There are a dozen other good places to stand, and the sculptor planned for all of them.

He was a foreigner. Jean de Boulogne was born in Flanders in 1529, traveled to Italy around the age of twenty to study ancient statues, and never went home. The Italians bent his name into Giambologna. He became the favorite sculptor of the Medici, the family that ruled Florence.
From any side, the group reads as a twist.

lines.label: The spiral
lines.text: Start at the crouching man's head, climb the standing man's back, swing across the woman's body and out through her raised hand. The line never runs straight.

lines.label: The crossing
lines.text: Her body lies across the climb. His hand clamps her hip on the left, and her free arm falls open on the right, so the group spreads out as it rises.

lesson.text: Sculptors of the time had a name for this corkscrew: figura serpentinata, the snake-like figure. It belongs to Mannerism, a style of the 1500s that loved difficulty, elegance and bodies turned further than bodies turn. A twisting statue has no front. To finish seeing it, you have to walk.
This group is designed to be seen from every side, with no single main view. The spiral makes your feet do part of the looking.

Here is the odd part. When Giambologna carved it, the group had no subject. He wanted to prove that he could lock three figures into one rising block: an old man, a young man and a woman. What story they were acting out, he left for later.

The title was supplied afterward by a Florentine writer, Raffaello Borghini. He proposed the legend of the first Romans, who were short of wives and carried off the women of their neighbors, the Sabines. A bronze relief of that story was then added to the base to settle the matter.

lesson.title: Marble pretending
lesson.text: With the story out of the way, what remains is what Giambologna cared about: stone behaving like flesh.

spots.title: A hand in the sky
spots.text: Her open hand is the highest point of the group, fingers spread against the blue. Each finger is free-standing marble, the thickness of a real finger.

spots.title: The grip
spots.text: His fingers sink into her side, and the stone seems to give under them like skin. Nothing here is soft. It is all one hard, cold material.

spots.title: Her profile
spots.text: Head thrown back over her shoulder, lips parted, tight curls deeply drilled. She looks away from both men, out over the square.

lesson.text: That pressed flesh was a new kind of showing off, and other sculptors took note. Some forty years later in Rome, the young Bernini carved his own abduction, with a god's fingers digging into a thigh. He had studied Giambologna's trick.

Before touching the marble, Giambologna built the whole group at full size as a model. It survives. You can see it indoors in Florence, at the Accademia, the same museum that houses Michelangelo's David.
So far you have met two of the three figures. The third is easy to miss from this angle, because he is in shadow and because the eye keeps racing upward.
An older man crouches under the other two. Where is his head?

spots.title: The man underneath
spots.text: A dark, curly head twists upward at the lower right. Just above it, one hand is raised with fingers spread, as if to shield himself from what is happening overhead.

lesson.text: Trapped between the younger man's legs, he is the loser of the scene, perhaps a father or a husband. He also does a mason's job: his bent body is the wide, low mass that lets the rest climb so high.

The statue has stood since 1583 in the Loggia dei Lanzi, an open arcade on the Piazza della Signoria, free to anyone crossing the square. If you go, start where this photo was taken. Then circle the group slowly, and count how many different sculptures you see.

quiz.question: How many blocks of marble make up the group?
quiz.explanation: All three figures are carved from a single block.

quiz.question: What does “figura serpentinata” describe?
options: A statue with snakes in its hair
A figure that twists upward in a spiral
A relief carved on a column
quiz.explanation: It is the snake-like, spiraling pose favored by Mannerist sculptors.

quiz.question: When did the group receive its subject?
options: It was dictated by the Medici
After it was carved, on a writer's suggestion
quiz.explanation: Giambologna carved it as a display of skill, and Raffaello Borghini proposed the Sabine story afterward.

quiz.question: Where was Giambologna born?
quiz.explanation: He was born Jean de Boulogne in Flanders and settled in Italy.

quiz.question: Why should you walk around this sculpture?
options: It has no single main view
quiz.explanation: It was designed to be seen from every side.

facts.text: Giambologna chose the Sabine story first and then designed the figures to fit it.
facts.explanation: He carved the group without a subject; the title came afterward.

facts.text: The full-size model for the group still exists in Florence.
facts.explanation: It is kept indoors at the Accademia.

facts.text: The statue is kept inside a museum, behind glass.
facts.explanation: It stands in the open Loggia dei Lanzi on the Piazza della Signoria.
